clinical_note:
INPATIENT NEUROREHABILITATION PROGRESS NOTE
Patient: 71-year-old male | Hospital Day 6 (Rehabilitation Day 2)
Primary Diagnosis: Acute left middle cerebral artery (M1) ischemic stroke status post intravenous tenecteplase and mechanical thrombectomy (TICI 2b recanalization).

Clinical Course:
The patient presented with an admission NIHSS of 14 and demonstrated partial neurological recovery following reperfusion therapy. On transfer to acute neurorehabilitation, bedside dysphagia screening failed due to delayed pharyngeal swallow initiation, wet vocal quality, and weak volitional cough; strict NPO status was ordered pending videofluoroscopic swallow study (VFSS) and nasogastric tube (NGT) placement. Three hours prior to evaluation, a visitor inadvertently provided approximately 120 mL of thin water by cup, followed by an episode of coughing and transient oxygen desaturation. Over the past two hours, the patient has become febrile, tachypneic, and increasingly fatigued.

Vital Signs:
Temperature 38.4 C, Heart Rate 112 bpm (sinus tachycardia), Blood Pressure 148/86 mmHg, Respiratory Rate 24 breaths/min, SpO2 89% on room air (improved to 94% on 3 L/min nasal cannula).

Physical and Neurological Examination:
Alert but fatigued; GCS 14 (E4V4M6; verbal limited by expressive aphasia). NIHSS 9 (unchanged from admission to rehab): right lower facial droop, Broca aphasia with intact single-step comprehension, right upper extremity strength 2/5, right lower extremity strength 3/5, mild right hemisensory loss. Pulmonary auscultation reveals coarse crackles and diminished breath sounds at the right lung base. Oral secretions pooling in posterior oropharynx.

Imaging and Laboratory Findings:
Portable chest radiograph (today): New patchy right lower lobe airspace consolidation with mild blunting of the right costophrenic angle, absent on Day 2 baseline film.
MRI brain (Day 2): Subacute left MCA territory infarction involving the insular cortex and left frontal operculum without hemorrhagic transformation or significant midline shift.
Labs: WBC 14.8 x10^9/L (84% neutrophils), hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL, platelets 264 x10^9/L, CRP 96 mg/L, procalcitonin 0.85 ng/mL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, serum sodium 138 mmol/L.

Current Medications:
- Aspirin 300 mg PR daily (substituted while NPO)
- Enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily
- Atorvastatin 80 mg daily (currently held pending enteral access)
- Intravenous 0.9% NaCl at 75 mL/h

Active Plan Notes:
Patient remains NPO; empiric antimicrobial coverage not yet initiated, and enteral access for nutrition and secondary stroke prevention medications remains pending.
ground_truth_red_flags: Acute hypoxemia (SpO2 89% on room air) with tachypnea (RR 24 breaths/min) and sinus tachycardia (HR 112 bpm)
New fever (38.4 C), neutrophilic leukocytosis (WBC 14.8 x10^9/L), elevated CRP/procalcitonin, and new right lower lobe consolidation on chest radiograph
Documented thin-liquid oral intake violating strict NPO precautions after failed bedside dysphagia screen with wet voice and pooled secretions
Delayed initiation of empiric antibiotics and lack of secured enteral access for nutrition and statin/antiplatelet therapy in a patient with Broca aphasia
ground_truth_differentials: Aspiration pneumonia
Hospital-acquired pneumonia
Acute pulmonary embolism

clinical_note:
NEUROSURGICAL INTERMEDIATE CARE PROGRESS NOTE
Patient: 58-year-old female | Postoperative Day 2
Primary Diagnosis: Right frontotemporal glioblastoma (WHO Grade 4) status post right frontotemporal craniotomy and subtotal resection.

Clinical Course:
The patient had an uncomplicated initial postoperative course and was extubated in the operating room with GCS 15 (E4V5M6) and intact motor strength throughout on Postoperative Day 1. Overnight, maintenance intravenous fluids were inadvertently transitioned to 0.45% NaCl at 100 mL/h. Over the past 90 minutes, nursing noted progressive somnolence, worsening confusion, and reluctance to move the left arm.

Vital Signs:
Temperature 37.1 C, Heart Rate 52 bpm (sinus bradycardia, down from baseline 78 bpm), Blood Pressure 184/98 mmHg (widened pulse pressure, up from 126/74 mmHg), Respiratory Rate 11 breaths/min with irregular breathing pattern, SpO2 97% on 2 L/min nasal cannula.

Physical and Neurological Examination:
GCS 10 (E2V3M5): opens eyes only to noxious stimulus, utters inappropriate words, localizes pain with the right upper extremity. Cranial nerves: new right-sided anisocoria with right pupil 5 mm and sluggishly reactive to light versus left pupil 3 mm and briskly reactive. Motor: new left upper extremity weakness (3/5 with pronator drift) and left lower extremity weakness (4/5); right-sided strength 5/5. Craniotomy incision intact with mild tense subgaleal fullness beneath the dressing.

Imaging and Laboratory Findings:
Non-contrast head CT (Postoperative Day 1): Expected right frontotemporal resection cavity with minimal blood products, trace pneumocephalus, surrounding vasogenic edema, and 2 mm leftward midline shift. STAT repeat non-contrast head CT has been ordered and is pending transport.
Labs (today): Serum sodium 132 mmol/L (down from 139 mmol/L yesterday), potassium 4.0 mmol/L, creatinine 0.7 mg/dL, glucose 168 mg/dL, hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL, platelets 195 x10^9/L, INR 1.0, aPTT 27 s.

Current Medications:
- Dexamethasone 4 mg IV q6h
- Levetiracetam 1000 mg IV q12h
- Famotidine 20 mg IV q12h
- Acetaminophen 650 mg IV q6h PRN
- Intravenous 0.45% NaCl at 100 mL/h (ongoing)
- Sequential compression devices (pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis held per neurosurgery)
ground_truth_red_flags: Acute neurological deterioration with GCS decline from 15 to 10 (E2V3M5)
New right-sided anisocoria (5 mm sluggish vs 3 mm brisk) with contralateral left hemiparesis indicating impending uncal herniation
Cushing triad physiology (hypertension 184/98 mmHg, new bradycardia 52 bpm, irregular bradypnea 11 breaths/min) signaling critically elevated intracranial pressure
Acute hyponatremia (serum sodium drop from 139 to 132 mmol/L) exacerbated by ongoing hypotonic 0.45% NaCl infusion in a post-craniotomy patient
ground_truth_differentials: Postoperative intracranial hemorrhage (epidural or resection-cavity hematoma)
Malignant postoperative cerebral edema with impending uncal herniation
Non-convulsive status epilepticus

clinical_note:
RESPIRATORY MEDICINE PROGRESS NOTE
Patient: 66-year-old female | Hospital Day 2
Primary Diagnosis: Acute exacerbation of severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD, GOLD Stage IV, Group E; baseline FEV1 28% predicted, chronic home oxygen 2 L/min targeting SpO2 88-92%).

Clinical Course:
Admitted with three days of escalating dyspnea, increased sputum volume and purulence, and diffuse wheezing. Baseline ambulatory arterial blood gas from pulmonary clinic showed compensated chronic hypercapnia (pH 7.38, PaCO2 54 mmHg, HCO3 31 mmol/L). Four hours ago, supplemental oxygen was escalated from 2 L/min nasal cannula to 6 L/min via simple face mask after a transient SpO2 reading of 87%. Two hours ago, the patient became acutely anxious and agitated and received lorazepam 1 mg IV. She is now markedly somnolent and difficult to arouse.

Vital Signs:
Temperature 37.9 C, Heart Rate 118 bpm (sinus tachycardia), Blood Pressure 156/92 mmHg, Respiratory Rate 28 breaths/min, SpO2 97% on 6 L/min simple face mask.

Physical and Neurological Examination:
Somnolent, arouses briefly to voice and vigorous sternal rub; GCS 13 (E3V4M6). Bilateral asterixis present on attempted wrist dorsiflexion. Respiratory exam demonstrates prominent sternocleidomastoid accessory muscle recruitment, pursed-lip breathing, paradoxical inward abdominal motion during inspiration, severely diminished air entry bilaterally, and faint end-expiratory wheezes. No peripheral edema; JVP not elevated.

Imaging and Laboratory Findings:
Arterial Blood Gas (on 6 L/min face mask): pH 7.24, PaCO2 78 mmHg, PaO2 94 mmHg, HCO3 32 mmol/L, SaO2 96%, lactate 2.1 mmol/L.
Portable chest radiograph: Marked pulmonary hyperinflation, flattened hemidiaphragms, increased retrosternal airspace, no focal lobar consolidation, no pleural effusion, no pneumothorax.
Labs: WBC 12.1 x10^9/L, hemoglobin 15.6 g/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, BNP 190 pg/mL, high-sensitivity troponin I <10 ng/L.

Current Medications:
- Albuterol 2.5 mg / ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulized q4h
- Methylprednisolone 40 mg IV daily
- Azithromycin 500 mg IV daily
- Enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily
- Lorazepam 1 mg IV (administered 2 hours prior)
- Supplemental oxygen 6 L/min via simple face mask
ground_truth_red_flags: Severe acute-on-chronic uncompensated respiratory acidosis (pH 7.24, PaCO2 78 mmHg vs baseline 54 mmHg) with hypercapnic encephalopathy (somnolence, GCS 13, asterixis)

Impending ventilatory arrest with accessory muscle fatigue and paradoxical abdominal motion (RR 28 breaths/min) requiring urgent noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation (BiPAP) or endotracheal intubation assessment
Excessive supplemental oxygen delivery (SpO2 97%, PaO2 94 mmHg on 6 L/min) exceeding the 88-92% COPD target and worsening hypercapnia via V/Q mismatch and the Haldane effect
Iatrogenic central respiratory depression following intravenous lorazepam administration in acute hypercapnic respiratory failure
ground_truth_differentials: Acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure secondary to COPD exacerbation
Iatrogenic hypercapnic narcosis from hyperoxia and benzodiazepine administration
Acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary edema

clinical_note:
SPINAL CORD INJURY REHABILITATION PROGRESS NOTE
Patient: 34-year-old male | 5 Weeks Post-Injury (Rehabilitation Day 19)
Primary Diagnosis: Traumatic cervical spinal cord injury, C5 neurological level, AIS A (complete tetraplegia), status post C5-C6 anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF).

Clinical Course:
Baseline hemodynamic profile since rehabilitation admission has been characterized by neurogenic hypotension (resting BP 92-100/54-62 mmHg, HR 60-68 bpm), managed with compression stockings, abdominal binder, and oral midodrine prior to upright therapy. During morning seated occupational therapy, the patient abruptly developed a severe pounding occipital headache, blurred vision, nasal congestion, and intense anxiety.

Vital Signs:
Temperature 36.8 C, Heart Rate 46 bpm (new sinus bradycardia), Blood Pressure 198/114 mmHg (systolic elevation >100 mmHg above baseline), Respiratory Rate 20 breaths/min, SpO2 96% on room air.

Physical and Neurological Examination:
Alert and oriented, visibly distressed; GCS 15 (E4V5M6). Profuse diaphoresis, cutaneous flushing, and piloerection noted across the face, neck, and upper chest above the C5 sensory level, with cool, pale skin below the level of injury. Neurological exam unchanged from baseline C5 AIS A (biceps 4/5 bilaterally, wrist extensors 1/5, absent motor and sensory function below C5). Abdominal exam reveals firm suprapubic fullness with palpable bladder distension. Inspection of the indwelling 16 Fr Foley catheter demonstrates a tight kink in the drainage tubing compressed beneath the wheelchair cushion, with zero urine output recorded in the collection bag over the last four hours. Nursing chart confirms last documented bowel movement was four days ago.

Imaging and Laboratory Findings:
MRI cervical spine (4 weeks prior): Focal C5 spinal cord contusion with early myelomalacia and intact anterior surgical hardware without epidural compression.
Labs (2 days prior): Creatinine 0.6 mg/dL, serum sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, urinalysis pending.

Current Medications:
- Midodrine 5 mg PO TID (last dose given 2 hours ago; next dose scheduled)
- Baclofen 10 mg PO TID
- Gabapentin 300 mg PO TID
- Oxybutynin 5 mg PO BID
- Enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily
- Senna 17.2 mg PO nightly and docusate 100 mg PO BID
ground_truth_red_flags: Life-threatening autonomic dysreflexia with severe paroxysmal hypertension (BP 198/114 mmHg vs baseline 96/58 mmHg), reflex bradycardia (HR 46 bpm), pounding headache, blurred vision, and supralesional diaphoresis/flushing
Acute urinary retention from kinked Foley catheter with four hours of anuria and palpable suprapubic bladder distension acting as primary noxious trigger
Four-day obstipation representing potential fecal impaction as an additional noxious stimulus below the T6 level
Active standing order for midodrine (alpha-1 adrenergic agonist), which is contraindicated during acute hypertensive crisis and autonomic dysreflexia
ground_truth_differentials: Autonomic dysreflexia triggered by acute urinary retention and possible fecal impaction
Intracerebral hemorrhage or hypertensive encephalopathy
Acute urosepsis with neurogenic bladder outlet obstruction

clinical_note:
RESPIRATORY WEANING UNIT PROGRESS NOTE
Patient: 52-year-old male | Hospital Day 21
Primary Diagnosis: Severe Guillain-Barre syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy with secondary axonal features) following Campylobacter jejuni gastroenteritis, status post five-day IVIG course (0.4 g/kg/day) and percutaneous tracheostomy on Hospital Day 12.

Clinical Course:
The patient was transferred to the specialized respiratory weaning unit for progressive liberation from mechanical ventilation. Yesterday he tolerated two hours of pressure-support ventilation (PSV) with FVC 17 mL/kg and negative inspiratory force (NIF) -28 cmH2O. Today, 45 minutes into a PSV weaning trial (PS 8 cmH2O, PEEP 5 cmH2O, FiO2 0.30), he developed acute diaphoresis, rapid shallow breathing, inability to clear thick tracheal secretions, and pronounced hemodynamic instability on continuous telemetry.

Vital Signs:
Temperature 37.3 C, Heart Rate labile between 44 bpm and 134 bpm (telemetry recorded two 2.8-second sinus pauses following tracheal suctioning), Blood Pressure fluctuating abruptly between 84/50 mmHg and 192/106 mmHg within 20 minutes, Respiratory Rate 34 breaths/min (exhaled tidal volume 250 mL; Rapid Shallow Breathing Index 136 breaths/min/L), SpO2 91% on FiO2 0.30.

Physical and Neurological Examination:
Alert, anxious, communicating via eye blinks and mouthing words; GCS 11T (E4VTM6). Bilateral facial diplegia and severe quadriparesis (1/5 proximal and distal extremities, diffuse areflexia). Pulmonary auscultation shows coarse transmitted rhonchi and decreased breath sounds at the left base; weak cough reflex on suctioning.

Imaging and Laboratory Findings:
Bedside Respiratory Mechanics: Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) 11 mL/kg (780 mL, decreased from 17 mL/kg yesterday), NIF (MIP) -18 cmH2O (worsened from -28 cmH2O), peak cough flow 120 L/min.
Arterial Blood Gas (on PSV, FiO2 0.30): pH 7.32, PaCO2 52 mmHg, PaO2 64 mmHg, HCO3 26 mmol/L.
Portable chest radiograph: New patchy left lower lobe atelectasis; tracheostomy tube tip positioned appropriately 3.5 cm above the carina; no pneumothorax.
Labs: Potassium 4.3 mmol/L, magnesium 1.9 mg/dL, phosphate 3.1 mg/dL, WBC 9.4 x10^9/L, TSH 1.8 mIU/L.

Current Medications:
- Metoprolol tartrate 25 mg via PEG BID (initiated 2 days ago for paroxysmal tachycardia)
- Gabapentin 600 mg via PEG TID
- Enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily
- Albuterol 2.5 mg / ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulized via inline circuit q6h
- Lubricating eye ointment q4h and scheduled chest physiotherapy
ground_truth_red_flags: Severe cardiovascular dysautonomia with extreme blood pressure lability (84/50 to 192/106 mmHg) and 2.8-second sinus pauses triggered by tracheal suctioning
Acute ventilator weaning failure and neuromuscular respiratory deterioration (FVC 11 mL/kg, NIF -18 cmH2O, RSBI 136 breaths/min/L, acute respiratory acidosis pH 7.32, PaCO2 52 mmHg)
Severely impaired airway clearance (peak cough flow 120 L/min) with evolving left lower lobe atelectasis and hypoxemia (PaO2 64 mmHg, SpO2 91%)
Scheduled oral beta-blocker (metoprolol tartrate 25 mg BID) posing high risk of profound bradycardia, hypotension, or asystole amid GBS dysautonomia and sinus pauses
ground_truth_differentials: Neuromuscular respiratory muscle fatigue and weaning failure secondary to Guillain-Barre syndrome
Severe Guillain-Barre syndrome-associated cardiovascular dysautonomia
Mucus plugging with lobar atelectasis or early ventilator-associated pneumonia

clinical_note:
NEUROCRITICAL CARE PROGRESS NOTE
Patient: 54-year-old female | Post-Bleed Day 7
Primary Diagnosis: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (Hunt-Hess Grade 3, modified Fisher Grade 4) from a ruptured 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm status post endovascular coil embolization on Day 1 and right frontal external ventricular drain (EVD) placement.

Clinical Course:
The patient stabilized after aneurysm securing and had been following commands consistently with GCS 14 (E4V4M6) and symmetric 5/5 strength through Post-Bleed Day 6. Earlier today, norepinephrine infusion was discontinued after spontaneous blood pressure elevation. Forty-five minutes after her scheduled enteral nimodipine 60 mg dose, systemic blood pressure fell abruptly. Over the last three hours, she has become markedly abulic, confused, and slow to respond, with new weakness of the right leg.

Vital Signs:
Temperature 38.2 C, Heart Rate 104 bpm, Blood Pressure 114/64 mmHg (MAP 81 mmHg, decreased from 158/86 mmHg two hours ago), Respiratory Rate 18 breaths/min, SpO2 98% on room air. Intracranial pressure (ICP) 12 mmHg with EVD open at 15 cmH2O above the tragus draining 14 mL/h of clear xanthochromic CSF.

Physical and Neurological Examination:
GCS 12 (E3V3M6): opens eyes to loud voice, speaks confused single words with marked latency (abulia), follows simple motor commands intermittently. Pupils 3 mm equal and briskly reactive. Mild dysarthria. Motor exam reveals new right lower extremity paresis (3/5 hip flexion and knee extension) with right upper extremity 4+/5 and intact left-sided 5/5 strength. Mucous membranes appear dry; 24-hour fluid balance is negative 1.4 L despite ongoing IV fluids.

Imaging and Laboratory Findings:
Transcranial Doppler (TCD, today): Left anterior cerebral artery (ACA) mean flow velocity 168 cm/s (increased from 92 cm/s yesterday); left middle cerebral artery (MCA) mean flow velocity 196 cm/s with Lindegaard ratio 4.6 (consistent with severe vasospasm).
Non-contrast head CT (4 hours ago): Resolving basal cistern and interhemispheric blood, no rebleeding, no new infarction, stable ventricular caliber with EVD tip in right frontal horn.
Labs: Serum sodium 127 mmol/L (down from 135 mmol/L 24 hours ago), serum osmolality 264 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 118 mmol/L, urine osmolality 510 mOsm/kg, BUN 26 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, WBC 11.8 x10^9/L.

Current Medications:
- Nimodipine 60 mg via nasogastric tube q4h
- Levetiracetam 500 mg IV q12h
- Intravenous 0.9% NaCl at 75 mL/h
- Acetaminophen 650 mg via NG q6h PRN
ground_truth_red_flags: Acute focal neurological deterioration on Post-Bleed Day 7 (GCS drop from 14 to 12, new abulia and right lower extremity paresis 3/5 characteristic of ACA territory ischemia)
Transcranial Doppler evidence of severe cerebral vasospasm (left ACA MFV 168 cm/s, left MCA MFV 196 cm/s, Lindegaard ratio 4.6)
Post-nimodipine systemic blood pressure drop (158/86 to 114/64 mmHg, MAP 81 mmHg) compromising cerebral perfusion pressure across vasospastic vessels
Severe hypovolemic hyponatremia (serum sodium 127 mmol/L, urine sodium 118 mmol/L, 24-hour fluid balance -1.4 L) consistent with cerebral salt wasting worsening cerebral ischemia risk
ground_truth_differentials: Delayed cerebral ischemia secondary to severe cerebral vasospasm
Cerebral salt wasting causing symptomatic hyponatremia and intravascular volume depletion
EVD-associated ventriculitis or early acute hydrocephalus

clinical_note:
NEUROREHABILITATION DISCHARGE / ACUTE TRANSFER SUMMARY
Patient: 27-year-old male | Day 24 Post-Trauma (Rehabilitation Day 8)
Primary Diagnosis: Severe traumatic brain injury (motor vehicle collision; initial GCS 6) with bilateral frontal hemorrhagic contusions and Grade II diffuse axonal injury, managed non-operatively with temporary ICP monitoring, PEG tube, and tracheostomy (now decannulated).

Clinical Course:
The patient was admitted to inpatient brain injury rehabilitation at Rancho Los Amigos Level IV (confused-agitated) with baseline GCS 11 (E4V2M5). Over the past 24 hours, he experienced five stereotypical paroxysmal episodes lasting 25 to 40 minutes, consistently provoked by oropharyngeal suctioning, turning, or passive limb stretching. Each episode involved severe hyperthermia, marked tachycardia, hypertension, profuse sweating, and bilateral extensor (decerebrate) posturing. For severe agitation overnight, the cross-covering clinician administered haloperidol 5 mg IM twice over 12 hours. Following the second dose, diffuse muscular rigidity persisted even between paroxysms, and urine output turned dark amber.

Vital Signs (during current episode):
Temperature 39.6 C, Heart Rate 148 bpm (sinus tachycardia), Blood Pressure 178/104 mmHg, Respiratory Rate 34 breaths/min, SpO2 94% on 2 L/min nasal cannula.

Physical and Neurological Examination:
GCS 9 (E3V2M4; deteriorated from baseline 11). Diaphoretic and flushed with severe generalized lead-pipe rigidity superimposed on intermittent extensor posturing of all four extremities. Pupils 5 mm equal and reactive. Lungs clear to auscultation without focal crackles. Abdomen soft; PEG site clean without erythema.

Imaging and Laboratory Findings:
Labs (today): Creatine kinase (CK) 4,850 U/L (up from 420 U/L three days ago), serum creatinine 1.4 mg/dL (baseline 0.8 mg/dL), potassium 5.1 mmol/L, WBC 11.4 x10^9/L, venous lactate 3.2 mmol/L, AST 186 U/L, ALT 94 U/L. Urinalysis: dark amber, 3+ blood on dipstick, 0-2 RBCs/HPF on microscopy (consistent with myoglobinuria), leukocyte esterase and nitrites negative.
MRI brain (Day 14): Evolving bilateral frontal contusions and corpus callosum/dorsolateral brainstem microhemorrhages consistent with diffuse axonal injury; normal ventricular size, no midline shift.

Current Medications:
- Propranolol 20 mg via PEG TID
- Clonidine 0.1 mg via PEG TID
- Levetiracetam 500 mg via PEG BID
- Enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily
- Haloperidol 5 mg IM q6h PRN agitation (two doses administered in past 12 hours)
ground_truth_red_flags: Severe uncontrolled sympathetic hyperarousal with hyperthermia (39.6 C), tachycardia (148 bpm), tachypnea (34 breaths/min), hypertension (178/104 mmHg), extensor posturing, and persistent lead-pipe rigidity
Acute rhabdomyolysis (CK 4,850 U/L, dipstick-positive myoglobinuria without microscopic hematuria) complicated by acute kidney injury (creatinine 1.4 mg/dL) and rising potassium (5.1 mmol/L)
Administration of haloperidol (5 mg IM x2) in a severe traumatic brain injury patient, which impairs neurorecovery, lowers seizure threshold, and can precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Decline in level of consciousness from baseline GCS 11 to GCS 9 with lactic acidosis (lactate 3.2 mmol/L) requiring immediate ICU-level transfer
ground_truth_differentials: Paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity (dysautonomia) secondary to severe traumatic brain injury
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome precipitated by haloperidol administration
Systemic sepsis or occult central nervous system infection

clinical_note:
ACUTE NEUROLOGY / NEUROSURGERY ICU PROGRESS NOTE
Patient: 63-year-old male | Hospital Day 2 (36 Hours Post-Symptom Onset)
Primary Diagnosis: Acute right posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) and superior cerebellar artery (SCA) ischemic stroke.

Clinical Course:
The patient presented 14 hours after sudden onset of severe vertigo, nausea, dysarthria, and truncal ataxia, outside the therapeutic window for intravenous thrombolysis or endovascular thrombectomy. Admission NIHSS was 4 and GCS was 15 (E4V5M6). Admission MRI confirmed a large acute infarction involving the right cerebellar hemisphere. Over the past two hours, he developed escalating occipital headache, three episodes of forceful vomiting, progressive drowsiness, and horizontal diplopia.

Vital Signs:
Temperature 37.0 C, Heart Rate 56 bpm (decreased from 82 bpm six hours prior), Blood Pressure 176/94 mmHg (increased from 142/80 mmHg), Respiratory Rate 14 breaths/min, SpO2 96% on room air.

Physical and Neurological Examination:
GCS 11 (E2V4M5): opens eyes to painful stimulus, confused speech, localizes pain symmetrically. Cranial nerves: new right abducens (CN VI) palsy with impaired right lateral gaze; gaze-evoked nystagmus; pupils 3 mm equal and reactive. Motor: moves all extremities symmetrically (5/5) when stimulated, severe right limb dysmetria, new bilateral extensor plantar responses (Babinski signs).

Imaging and Laboratory Findings:
Repeat non-contrast head CT (completed 30 minutes ago): Enlarging acute right cerebellar hypodensity with marked posterior fossa mass effect, complete effacement of the fourth ventricle and quadrigeminal cistern, leftward displacement of the pons and medulla, and early enlargement of the temporal horns of the lateral ventricles consistent with acute obstructive hydrocephalus. No hemorrhagic transformation.
Labs: Serum sodium 138 mmol/L, glucose 142 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL, platelets 228 x10^9/L, INR 1.1.

Current Medications:
- Aspirin 325 mg PO daily
- Atorvastatin 80 mg PO daily
- Unfractionated heparin 5000 units SC q8h
- Ondansetron 4 mg IV q6h PRN
- Intravenous 0.9% NaCl at 75 mL/h

Active Plan Notes:
Repeat head CT was uploaded 30 minutes ago; hyperosmolar therapy has not yet been administered and neurosurgical re-evaluation for urgent decompression has not yet been requested.
ground_truth_red_flags: Rapid neurological deterioration (GCS decline from 15 to 11) with intractable vomiting, new right CN VI palsy, and bilateral Babinski signs indicating acute brainstem compression
Repeat head CT demonstrating malignant cerebellar edema with complete fourth ventricle effacement, brainstem shift, and early acute obstructive hydrocephalus
Emerging Cushing response (heart rate drop from 82 to 56 bpm with rising blood pressure 176/94 mmHg) signaling impending tonsillar or upward transtentorial herniation
Unacted-upon critical neuroimaging findings with delayed neurosurgical escalation for suboccipital decompressive craniectomy and absence of bridge hyperosmolar therapy
ground_truth_differentials: Malignant cerebellar edema with acute obstructive hydrocephalus and brainstem compression
Basilar artery thrombosis with acute brainstem ischemia
Delayed hemorrhagic transformation of cerebellar infarction

clinical_note:
RESPIRATORY STEP-DOWN DISCHARGE / ESCALATION SUMMARY
Patient: 62-year-old female | Hospital Day 5 (18 Days Post-Ischemic Stroke)
Primary Diagnosis: Acute saddle pulmonary embolism; recent right hemispheric ischemic stroke (18 days prior, residual mild left leg weakness 4/5, NIHSS 3).

Clinical Course:
The patient was originally admitted to the respiratory step-down unit five days ago for suspected community-acquired pneumonia during subacute stroke recovery. During medication reconciliation on transfer, pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis was inadvertently omitted while the patient remained largely bedbound due to left lower extremity paresis. One hour ago, upon attempting to stand for bedside physical therapy, she experienced acute right-sided pleuritic chest pain, severe dyspnea, and near-syncope.

Vital Signs:
Temperature 37.4 C, Heart Rate 126 bpm (sinus tachycardia), Blood Pressure 92/58 mmHg (down from baseline 134/78 mmHg; MAP 69 mmHg), Respiratory Rate 30 breaths/min, SpO2 84% on room air, improving only to 89% on 6 L/min nasal cannula; escalated to high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) at 50 L/min and FiO2 0.70 with current SpO2 93%.

Physical and Neurological Examination:
Alert, anxious, diaphoretic, speaking in short phrases; GCS 15 (E4V5M6). Neck veins distended to the angle of the jaw at 45 degrees. Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally without wheezes or crackles. Extremities cool with capillary refill 3.5 seconds; mild asymmetric swelling and calf tenderness of the left lower extremity. Neurological exam unchanged with chronic left leg 4/5 strength.

Imaging and Laboratory Findings:
CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA, STAT): Large saddle embolus straddling the main pulmonary artery bifurcation with extensive bilateral lobar clot burden; right ventricular to left ventricular (RV/LV) diameter ratio 1.4 with interventricular septal flattening and contrast reflux into the inferior vena cava.
12-Lead ECG: Sinus tachycardia at 126 bpm, S1Q3T3 pattern, new T-wave inversions across precordial leads V1-V4.
Labs: High-sensitivity troponin I 412 ng/L (reference <14 ng/L), NT-proBNP 3,840 pg/mL, venous lactate 3.8 mmol/L, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, platelets 240 x10^9/L, INR 1.0.

Current Medications:
- Clopidogrel 75 mg PO daily
- Rosuvastatin 40 mg PO daily
- Lisinopril 10 mg PO daily (still listed as scheduled)
- Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily (empiric for presumed pneumonia)
- No systemic anticoagulation or VTE prophylaxis administered over the past 5 days
ground_truth_red_flags: Acute severe hypoxemia (SpO2 84% on room air requiring HFNC at 50 L/min, FiO2 0.70) with severe tachypnea (RR 30 breaths/min)
Obstructive shock physiology and impending hemodynamic collapse (BP 92/58 mmHg, HR 126 bpm, near-syncope, cool extremities, JVD, lactate 3.8 mmol/L)
Saddle pulmonary embolism with severe right ventricular dysfunction (RV/LV ratio 1.4, septal flattening, troponin I 412 ng/L, NT-proBNP 3,840 pg/mL)

Recent ischemic stroke 18 days ago constituting a major contraindication to systemic thrombolysis, necessitating immediate PERT activation for catheter-directed mechanical thrombectomy and careful anticoagulation evaluation, plus holding scheduled lisinopril
ground_truth_differentials: Acute high-risk (massive) saddle pulmonary embolism with right ventricular failure
Acute coronary syndrome / non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction
Cardiac tamponade or acute aortic dissection

clinical_note:
NEUROREHABILITATION DISCHARGE / ACUTE TRANSFER SUMMARY
Patient: 64-year-old female | Rehabilitation Day 9
Primary Diagnosis: Acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis admitted for multidisciplinary neurorehabilitation following corticosteroid-induced myopathy and deconditioning.

Clinical Course:
The patient was progressing well with graded endurance training and had stable bulbar and respiratory function through Rehabilitation Day 6 (baseline single-breath count 32, bedside FVC 28 mL/kg). Two days ago, oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg BID was initiated for mild dysuria and a urine culture positive for pansusceptible Escherichia coli. Over the past 18 hours, she developed rapidly worsening bilateral ptosis, nasal dysarthria, difficulty swallowing her own saliva, inability to lift her head off the pillow, and severe orthopnea requiring upright posture.

Vital Signs:
Temperature 37.2 C, Heart Rate 108 bpm, Blood Pressure 146/84 mmHg, Respiratory Rate 26 breaths/min (shallow inspirations), SpO2 93% on room air.

Physical and Neurological Examination:
Alert, fatigued, visibly anxious; GCS 15 (E4V5M6). Marked bilateral fatigable ptosis, weak orbicularis oculi closure, severe nasal dysarthria, and pooling of oral secretions with weak cough. Neck flexor strength 2/5 (markedly declined from 4/5 two days prior); proximal shoulder abduction 3/5 with rapid fatigability. Respiratory exam demonstrates shallow tidal volumes, sternocleidomastoid recruitment, and paradoxical abdominal movement when supine. No fasciculations, miosis, bronchorrhea, or bradycardia.

Imaging and Laboratory Findings:
Bedside Neuromuscular Respiratory Testing: Single-breath count 11 (down from 32), Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) 14 mL/kg (840 mL, down from 28 mL/kg), Negative Inspiratory Force (NIF / MIP) -19 cmH2O.
Arterial Blood Gas (room air): pH 7.36, PaCO2 46 mmHg, PaO2 72 mmHg, HCO3 25 mmol/L.
Portable chest radiograph: Low lung volumes with bibasilar subsegmental atelectasis; no focal consolidation or pleural effusion.
Labs: WBC 8.9 x10^9/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, magnesium 2.4 mg/dL, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL.

Current Medications:
- Pyridostigmine 60 mg PO q4h while awake
- Prednisone 40 mg PO daily
- Mycophenolate mofetil 1000 mg PO BID
- Ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BID (Day 2 of 7)
- Magnesium oxide 400 mg PO daily (for constipation)
ground_truth_red_flags: Impending myasthenic crisis crossing critical intubation/ICU thresholds (FVC 14 mL/kg < 15-20 mL/kg, NIF -19 cmH2O worse than -20 to -30 cmH2O, single-breath count drop from 32 to 11)
Ominous rising PaCO2 (46 mmHg) despite tachypnea (RR 26 breaths/min) and paradoxical supine breathing, where preserved SpO2 (93%) is falsely reassuring for impending ventilatory arrest
Severe acute bulbar dysfunction (nasal dysarthria, pooled secretions, weak cough, neck flexor strength 2/5) carrying high aspiration and airway loss risk
Active administration of medications known to exacerbate neuromuscular junction blockade in myasthenia gravis (ciprofloxacin and magnesium oxide)
ground_truth_differentials: Impending myasthenic crisis triggered by fluoroquinolone and magnesium exposure
Cholinergic crisis secondary to pyridostigmine excess
Acute aspiration pneumonitis or early hospital-acquired pneumonia
